planting.note: Sow direct or plant divisions in early spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Blood-Veined Sorrel is grown as much for its striking red-veined foliage as for its edible, tangy leaves.

directions: Sow direct or plant divisions in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; a little afternoon shade helps the striking foliage color hold up better in hot summer weather. Blood-Veined Sorrel bears bright green leaves dramatically marked with deep red-purple veins, an ornamental pattern striking enough to earn it a spot in shade borders and mixed containers as well as the herb garden, while the young leaves carry the same tart, lemony flavor typical of sorrel and are edible raw in small amounts or cooked into soups and sauces. It tolerates more shade than most edible greens, making it a useful dual-purpose plant for a partly shaded kitchen garden bed. Remove flower stalks as they appear to prolong leaf quality and reduce self-seeding, and harvest young leaves continuously for the best flavor and most vivid color.

common_name: Green Carpet Pachysandra (Compact Dense Shade Groundcover)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant rooted divisions in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring; Green Carpet is a more compact, lower-growing selection than the straight species, forming a denser, tidier mat.

directions: Root stem cuttings or set out plugs in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing 6 to 8 inches apart. Green Carpet is a compact, low-growing selection of Japanese spurge that forms a denser, more uniform mat than the straight species, staying shorter and tidier while still providing the same reliable, evergreen, weed-suppressing groundcover for deep shade under trees where grass and most flowering groundcovers fail. Small white flower spikes appear in mid-spring, mostly hidden by the foliage. Requires acidic soil, since yellowing foliage in alkaline conditions signals the need for an acidifying soil amendment. It spreads steadily by underground stems once established and needs minimal care beyond occasional edging to control spread; watch for pachysandra blight in humid, poorly ventilated sites and avoid overhead watering.
